facts.claim: A surprisingly small number of tissue rhythms are lost when only local clocks are ablated.
facts.quote: First, a surprisingly small number of tissue rhythms are lost when only local clocks are ablated

facts.claim: Changing feeding times can change the phase of circadian gene expression in peripheral cell types by up to 12 h while leaving the SCN unaffected.
facts.quote: Here we show that temporal feeding restriction under light-dark or dark-dark conditions can change the phase of circadian gene expression in peripheral cell types by up to 12 h while leaving the phase of cyclic gene expression in the SCN unaffected.

facts.claim: Peripheral clocks act as gatekeepers that temporally adjust cellular responses to external stimuli.
facts.quote: peripheral clocks controlling some local rhythms while at the same time acting as gatekeepers that temporally adjust cellular responses to external stimuli.

facts.claim: Circadian clocks exist in nearly every body cell, not just in the brain's suprachiasmatic nucleus.
facts.quote: In mammals, the circadian timekeeping system has a complex architecture, composed of a central pacemaker in the brain's suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) and subsidiary clocks in nearly every body cell.

facts.claim: Food-induced phase resetting proceeds faster in liver than in kidney, heart, or pancreas.
facts.quote: Food-induced phase resetting proceeds faster in liver than in kidney, heart, or pancreas, but after 1 wk of daytime feeding, the phases of circadian gene expression are similar in all examined peripheral tissues.

facts.claim: Dysregulation of clock genes is linked to alterations in proliferation, metabolism, epithelial plasticity, immune regulation, metastatic potential, and treatment responsiveness in colorectal cancer.
facts.quote: statistically significant associations were consistently reported between dysregulation of clock genes such as PER1 , PER3 , CLOCK , BMAL1 , CRY1 , TIMELESS , and ARNTL2 and alterations in proliferation, metabolism, epithelial plasticity, immune regulation, metastatic potential, and treatment responsiveness.

research.angle: While the brain's SCN acts as a master pacemaker, nearly every cell in the body contains its own clock that can be independently adjusted by factors like metabolism and local signals.
research.verdict: The evidence confirms that circadian clocks are distributed throughout the body's tissues and can function independently of the central brain pacemaker.
research.caveat: The traditional hierarchical model is being replaced by a more integrated 'federated' model where local and systemic factors interact to regulate rhythms.
